title: MindMed's LSD for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Might Be A Success for...Medicaid?
subtitle: An argument about healthcare economics.
body_html:
Just last week, my friends from MindMed1 published a phase 2b study on their investigational compound, “MM-120,” which is an orally dissolving version of LSD. Yes, that LSD. The inspiration for Lucy-in-the-Sky-with-Diamonds-LSD. This article will break down what they found in their paper—published in JAMA!—and why I think this drug, and others like it, might actually be best understood as a turning point for Medicaid plans.

Select disclosures: I’ve been a PI for MindMed’s AI trials23 in the past, and hold about 500 shares of their stock! I’ve also been a compensated consultant to BrainFutures on the topic of scaling psychedelic therapies.4

What Is the History of LSD?

It’s times like this I’m thrilled I already wrote a paper on this topic5, excerpted here:

Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) was first synthesized by Albert Hoffman in 1938 as a potential central nervous system stimulant for use in recovery from anesthesia. An accidental laboratory exposure 5 years later resulted in a profound consciousness-altering experience, prompting Hoffman and colleagues to engage in further experimentation. The drug was subsequently promoted for use in analytical psychotherapy, where it was found to be effective for the treatment of alcohol use disorder (AUD).6 However, as the drug rose in popularity during the 1960s, recreational use triggered some instances of long-term psychosis.2 Sensationalized media reports, coupled with the role of LSD in the counterculture movement, sparked a moral panic from the establishment.7 Under the Controlled Substances Act of 1970, the Nixon administration classified LSD as a Schedule I drug, putting a halt to serious medical investigation for nearly 50 years.

The following study is the only large-scale modern clinical trial of an LSD compound (it’s a proprietary dissolving tablet studied by the team at MindMed). This initial study is for a GAD indication, but their phase III trials include both this FDA-Breakthrough pathway GAD indication, as well as separate phase III trials for MDD.

What Did Single Treatment With MM120 (Lysergide) in Generalized Anxiety Disorder Show?

This study is a phase 2b trial for FDA approval. As a quick reminder, phase 2b studies are part of the pathway to FDA approval that is designed to answer the following questions:

In phase two, drugs are given in various dosages to individuals with the disorder in question. It moves from humans without the illness to humans with the illness the drug is intended to treat. Again, using our imagined drug, “water,” we might give 1oz, 8oz, 16oz, 32oz, and 128oz in the phase two trial. Thirst-reduction was noted in individuals given 8oz and 16oz. Still, no effect was noted in the 1oz group, and excessive urination and abdominal distention were noted, along with slight changes in blood levels of sodium in the 128oz group.

When conducted well, the study sponsor has the data to determine the optimal design for their phase III trials (of which there need to be two for a drug approval).

Who was in this MindMed trial?

Of 198 participants randomized, 194 were included in the full analysis set (mean age, 41.3 [SD, 13.6] years; 56.7% were female; and 3.6% were Asian, 7.7% were Black or African American, and 83.0% were White).

And they were randomized to different doses:

Participants were randomized to receive a single (freebase equivalent) treatment dose with 25 µg (n = 39), 50 µg (n = 40), 100 µg (n = 40), or 200 µg (n = 40) of MM120 or placebo (n = 39).

The most important detail is, of course, the dosing regimen.

One dose was given. Once. With no “prep” work, no therapy, and no fancy integration thereafter. Just someone monitoring you for 12 hours while you have a psychedelic experience with the following adverse effects:

The most common adverse events were visual perceptual changes (illusion, pseudo-hallucination, and visual hallucination), which occurred in 46.2% of participants who received 25 µg of MM120, in 75.0% who received 50 µg, in 92.5% who received 100 µg, in 100% who received 200 µg, and in 10.3% who received placebo;

10.3% of placebo patients had visual perceptual changes! There were also less sexy Adverse Effects (like nausea and headache):

nausea occurred in 7.7%, 27.5%, 40.0%, 60.0%, and 7.7%, respectively; and headache occurred in 12.8%, 22.5%, 35.0%, 27.5%, and 23.1%.

And then, they got to watch a remarkable shift in anxiety unfold:

The dose-response relationship assessed using the MCP-Mod method for change in HAM-A score at week 4 was statistically significant for the 100-µg and the 200-µg dose groups vs placebo (least-squares mean difference, −5.0 points [95% CI, −9.6 to −0.4 points] with 100 µg of MM120 and −6.0 points [95% CI, −9.8 to −2.0 points] with 200 µg of MM120)

Which is pharma-trial speak for:

Clinical response rate of 78% in 100 µg and 200 µg dose groups and 50% clinical remission rate in the 100 µg dose group at Week 4.

Half of the participants experienced Remission of anxiety after one dose of a medicine, followed by no therapy, just living one’s life…let me put that in bigger type:

Anxiety was *Over* in 50% of Subjects after One Dose of MM-120.

It’s also worth mentioning their MDD phase 2b trial data (investigator-initiated) was similarly “a big deal” and has been “toplined”— but not yet published:

Patients in the high dose arm (n=28) demonstrated a least square mean change from baseline in IDS-C scores of -12.9 points compared to -3.6 points in the lower dose arm (n=27, p=0.02). The statistically significant benefit as measured by IDS-C was maintained up to 16 weeks after the first administration compared to placebo (p=0.008).

Why Does This Matter In Medicaid Populations?

Let’s start with the obvious…Anxiety is impairing. Here is the data on impairment from GAD presented by MindMed (who have a commercial interest in making sure we all know these data):

As you can imagine, having impairment at work is bad, and having impairment in your activities of daily life is also bad, and in the 30% range in severe GAD, I've got problems.

GAD: It’s prevalent in primary care populations:

World Health Organization study conducted in 15 countries reported that 7.9% of all primary care patients currently had GAD17

GAD is a driver of cost, dating back to 2013 data—it’s unlikely to have gotten less expensive:

8.74% of adult respondents reported being diagnosed with anxiety disorder(s). The annual overall healthcare expenditure associated with anxiety disorders was estimated at $1657.52 per person (SE: $238.83; p < 0.001). Inpatient visits, prescription medications, and office-based visits together accounted for almost 93% of the overall cost. …their total direct medical expenditure is estimated at approximately $33.71 billion in 2013 US dollars8

And we have a problem in Medicaid populations…expansion of coverage, at least in college students, led to more mental health services but not better outcomes:

We find that students from disadvantaged backgrounds are more likely to report being on public insurance after 2014 in expansion states relative to non-expansion states, while more advantaged students do not see this increase. Both diagnosis of common mental health conditions and psychotropic drug use increase following expansion for disadvantaged students relative to advantaged ones, which translates into an elimination of the pre-treatment gap in these outcomes by family background in expansion states. However, these changes are not associated with short-term improvements in measures of mental health status or academic outcomes.9

Thanks, economists! It’s a bummer that access to care doesn’t mean the care is helpful, at least in this sample, but that is also validating to your author, whose whole thesis for his life is “what we are doing isn’t good enough to address a very serious range of problems.”

We have one natural experiment in insurance coverage benefiting Medicaid individuals—the Oregon roll-out was done in an essentially randomized manner, as described in a delightful Freakonomics episode.

The lottery that expanded Medicaid allowed more people to get coverage, but it didn’t (broadly) lower costs:

I think a lot of people hung their hopes for expanding insurance on the idea that it would somehow pay for itself because you would cut out emergency department use and save so much money that way, that that money would then pay for all the other healthcare. It’s a much easier case to make if you can say it’ll also save money, so then you don’t force people to decide how much they value healthcare for other people. The only problem is that it’s just not true. When you expand insurance, people use more healthcare and that costs money.

However, at least when it comes to depression, there was a big difference in that Oregon data set:

We also did a clinical assessment of depression, and we found that Medicaid substantially reduced the incidence of depression. There was something like a 9 percentage point or 30 percent drop. So this is an enormous mental health benefit, and that’s a huge unmet health need in this population. But when we measured things like blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, we didn’t detect any improvements in those chronic physical health outcomes and this again, caused some consternation among proponents of expanding health insurance. It is a much more complicated story than simply saying, “Yes, insurance worked,” or, “No, it didn’t work.” It had some really beneficial effects, but it didn’t solve our problems with chronic physical health conditions.

But it did get depression better! People in remission don’t have that medical problem in their lives. People who are not anxious (in remission from GAD) are unlikely to have the impairments from Anxiety, just like when broken legs heal, people can walk again.

It’s also the case that people who are not avoiding work anymore, because their crippling anxiety has abated, are likely to get a job they can keep, and no longer be covered by Medicaid, which is good for state budgets.

One of the fundamental challenges of running a Medicaid health plan is that the amount of money is limited, at the state level, in a way federal spending is not. States can just print more money to pay for the runway healthcare expenses. Similarly, the most vulnerable individuals are on Medicaid, but often not for very long; the average amount of time on a Medicaid plan is measured in months, as I covered in detail previously.

It's tough to manage population health when you only have months to accomplish the goal:

We also found that Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries were enrolled for an average of 11.6 months over a 12-month enrollment span.

We don’t have the explicit data on anxiety in Medicaid like we do with depression; however, the co-morbidity alone is enough for me.

This brings us to the crux of my argument!

Single Dose Psychedelics That Lead To Remission Work Fast, and That Matters In Populations When There Is Little Time to Recognize Savings

MM-120, if approved, is a single-dose treatment with durability that could quickly realize its benefits in individuals on Medicaid, potentially accomplishing the almost impossible task of saving money in a Medicaid health plan.

If MM120 works in a single day and single dose, and people who don't have anxiety get back to work, that alone could reduce the number of Medicaid beneficiaries out of work. Similarly, even if someone is staying on Medicaid, but changing plans? Well, since MM120 works so quickly, the savings might be realized in the timeframe in which the individual is on the plan. They might have less “health anxiety,” for example, or any number of other possible outcomes. This story will get even stronger if MM120 gets a major depressive disorder indication.

People on Medicaid deserve great healthcare. But there are indeed limited resources, and those resources need to be stewarded appropriately. We might have a very rare combination of excellent outcomes, limited risks, and the ability to drive savings with one treatment if the data from the phase 2b trial is replicated in subsequent studies and into the real world.

More options for the most vulnerable individuals that are also good for state budgets?

I'll be watching closely!
